section.title: Continuity
section.p: The precise definition of a limit gave us a way to control nearby values. It said:

section.p: But a limit still does not have to care about the value at the point. A function may have a hole, a wrong value, or no value at all, and still have a limit nearby.
Continuity is the calm case. It is the case where the nearby behavior and the actual value agree.

exercise.title: What three things must happen for continuity at a point?

statement.p: Continuity at a means \lim_{x\to a}f(x)=f(a). In your own words, why does that one equation hide three requirements, and what goes wrong if the nearby limit exists but the actual value is missing or wrong?

hint.p: The output at a must exist, the nearby limit must exist, and those two numbers must agree. A hole or a relocated point breaks the last two in different ways.

note.title: Removable discontinuity
note.p: A function has a removable discontinuity at a if the limit
exists, but the function is not continuous at a because f(a) is missing or has the wrong value.

subsection.p: The word “removable” does not mean the original function was continuous. It means we can make it continuous by changing the value at one point.

exercise.title: When can a hole be repaired?

statement.p: The function \frac{x^2-1}{x-1} is not continuous at x=1 because the value is missing, yet defining the missing height to be 2 produces a continuous extension. In your own words, what makes a discontinuity removable, and why can a jump or a vertical asymptote not be repaired by filling in one point?

hint.p: Repair is possible only when nearby values already agree on a finite target. A jump has two targets. An infinite discontinuity has no finite target at all.

subsection.p: The one-sided conditions are natural. At the left endpoint a, points of the interval approach a only from the right. At the right endpoint b, points of the interval approach b only from the left.

exercise.title: Why do endpoints of a closed interval use one-sided continuity?

statement.p: Continuity on [a,b] asks for ordinary continuity inside (a,b), but only a right-hand match at a and a left-hand match at b. In your own words, why are those one-sided conditions the natural ones at the ends of a closed interval?

hint.p: At the left endpoint, allowed inputs of the interval approach only from the right. At the right endpoint, they approach only from the left. There is no other side inside the interval.

exercise.title: Why is continuity easy to build from old continuous pieces?

statement.p: Sums, products, and (when the denominator is nonzero) quotients of continuous functions are continuous, and so is a composition f\circ g when g is continuous at a and f is continuous at g(a). In your own words, why do these combination rules follow from limit laws, and why does a zero denominator still block continuity?

hint.p: Continuity says nearby values approach the actual values. Limit laws then pass that approach to sums, products, and compositions. A quotient is not even defined where the denominator is zero, so it cannot be continuous there.

exercise.title: Why can a composition have a limit when the inner function is not continuous?

statement.p: If \lim_{x\to a}g(x)=L and f is continuous at L, then \lim_{x\to a}f(g(x))=f(L), even if g has a hole or a wrong value at a. Why is the inner limit enough for the composition limit? Why is it not enough for continuity of f\circ g at a?

hint.p: Nearby values of g go to L, and a continuous outer function sends them to values near f(L). Continuity of the composition also needs f(g(a)) to exist and to equal that limit.

exercise.title: Why must the outer function be continuous at L?

statement.p: If \lim_{x\to a}g(x)=L but f is not continuous at L, then f(L) may not be the limit of f(g(x)). This is clearest when g(x)=L for every x. Why is a nearby limit of f not enough?

hint.p: A nearby limit of f ignores the value at L. If g equals L, the composition uses that ignored value.

exercise.title: If the inner limit fails, when can the composition still have a limit?

statement.p: The function |x|/x has no two-sided limit at 0. Neither does the identity of that function. Its square does. When does an inner jump remain after composition? When does it disappear?

hint.p: The jump remains if the two sides go to different heights. It disappears if they go to the same height.

subsection.title: Three common discontinuities
subsection.p: Continuity can fail in several ways. The three most common early failures are removable discontinuities, jump discontinuities, and infinite discontinuities.

md.mrow: \hline \text{removable} \amp \text{limit exists, but value is missing or wrong} \amp \displaystyle \frac{x^2-1}{x-1}\text{ at }x=1

figure.caption: Three common ways continuity can fail: a hole, a jump, or a vertical asymptote.

subsection.p: The names are not just vocabulary. They tell us what kind of repair, if any, is possible.
A removable discontinuity can be fixed by changing one value.
A jump cannot be fixed by changing one value, because the two sides approach different targets.
An infinite discontinuity cannot be fixed by changing one value, because nearby values do not stay near any finite number.

subsection.title: A continuity checklist
subsection.p: When checking continuity at a, ask:

row.cell: If not, the function is not continuous at a.
If the two sides disagree or the values do not settle, the function is not continuous at a.
If not, the nearby behavior and the actual value disagree.

subsection.p: For familiar formulas, continuity often lets us substitute directly. For piecewise functions, endpoints between pieces must be checked. For quotients, denominators must be watched. For roots and logarithms, the domain must be respected.

Continuity is still a local idea: it describes what happens near one point. But it has surprising global consequences. A continuous graph cannot jump over a height, and on a closed finite interval it cannot avoid having a highest and lowest point.
Those two facts are the next payoff.
